transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2027-01-05
Start Time (UTC): 15:30
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Gonzalez (CobaltFin Head of ML), Ethan Park (CobaltFin Infra), Li Wei (CobaltFin SRE)
Recording: https://app.fireflies.ai/recordings/ff-20270105-9b3a2f

Summary:
- Reviewed last week's TTFT regressions and new streaming microburst patterns; discussed kernel choice tradeoffs for seq len variance; agreed on profiling plan.
- Decided to run deeper microburst profiling at seq=512 and 1024, share anonymized traces, and hold kernel decision workshop next week.

Topics:
- TTFT vs sustained throughput tradeoffs
- Streaming handshake and first-token optimizations (fastpath vs full kv warm)
- Kernel selection: fused-attn kernels vs fallback matmul for certain seqlen ranges
- Sequence length distribution impact and hedging strategies
- Network egress/VPC constraints and cold-start timers

Action items (recap at end): Samir run profiling; Maya export traces; Ethan confirm networking window; Avery share docs/pricing.

Transcript:
[00:00] Avery: okay, let's get started. can everyone hear me?
[00:10] Maya: yep can hear, sorry just dialed in from home, noisy background.
[00:15] Samir: good, thanks. we'll run this tight 45, 50 minutes, we have three main points: ttft results, streaming microburst, kernel choices.
[00:30] Ethan: quick note, li is on for infra questions, li can chime in for peering and egress.
[00:36] Li: hi all.
[00:40] Avery: cool. Samir, do you want to take us through the TTFT numbers first?
[00:44] Samir: sure. so last week we saw the median TTFT for your demo traces drop to ~85ms but the p95 jumped to 420ms on microbursts, which aligned with the sequence length tail and cache misses. a couple of guesses: the continuous batching is causing larger 'wait' windows during bursty arrival patterns, and some requests are hitting a cold kv cache path that falls back to a slower fused kernel.
[01:10] Maya: yeah that matches what we're seeing - in the field there are short bursts when users open the app and we get big fanout so short-ish prompts then longer completions. what's puzzling is the first token is sometimes quick, sometimes late, we can't predict.
[01:25] Samir: right. we instrumented the path: fastpath allocates small kv warm cache, but if the incoming request goes straight to the generic matmul path it adds 200-300ms. our repro run shows a bimodal distribution.
[01:40] Ethan: is that kernel-specific? like fused attn for seqlen under 256 and matmul for above?
[01:45] Samir: sort of. our runtime picks kernels based on seqlen heuristics and hardware. there is a threshold where a quantized fused-attn is faster, but for some shapes the vendor kernel falls back. also tensor layout and batch shapes matter.
[02:02] Maya: can you say more about the caching path? i thought the KV cache warm-up persists across requests?
[02:09] Samir: it does if requests hit the same session and we have sticky routing. but with your fanout pattern we see many short-lived sessions; the prefix cache misses and we do a fresh kv allocation. that path has a different memory layout and triggers a fallback kernel.
[02:25] Li: from our side we also saw spikes when seq len jumps mid-request, eg user prompt plus long context retrieval. that causes more memory pressure and sometimes OOM retries which then throttle the node.
[02:36] Avery: important to call out the infra constraints - we heard earlier you have strict egress windows and peering maintenance nights, so we need to avoid tests during those times.
[02:45] Ethan: yes we have peering window 01:00–03:00 local, can't use that for heavy benchmarks.
[02:52] Samir: noted. okay, next i pulled a microburst trace from demo traffic. can i share my screen?
[02:58] Maya: go ahead.
[03:05] Samir: (screen) here's a timeline: blue bars are incoming QPS, orange lines are TTFT per request; you can see clusters where TTFT jumps to 400-600ms for a few seconds then normalizes. those correlate with new sessions and larger seqlen requests.
[03:25] Maya: hm, so it's not sustained; it's a microburst phenomenon. can we mitigate by batching differently?
[03:31] Samir: yes. there are two levers: reduce batching latency by lowering max batch window — which reduces TTFT but increases per-token compute inefficiency — or use pre-warmed reserved capacity with sticky routing which keeps kv cache hot but costs more.
[03:46] Ethan: what's the delta on cost for reserved capacity? rough order?
[03:50] Avery: i'll put numbers in the spreadsheet but ballpark is 20–40% more per-hour for a node with sticky sessions vs fully autoscaled. depends on utilization.
[04:02] Li: could we do opportunistic warming? like when we detect a spike pre-warm an instance?
[04:08] Samir: we have an option: lightweight prefetchers and prefix caching heuristics. but they only help if you can predict the session key space. with many ephemeral sessions prediction is harder.
[04:20] Maya: what about hedging? firing a fast low‑quality route first then fallback to full path?
[04:24] Samir: that's viable. we've used an early-response path: return a quick short token from a smaller quantized model or a smaller context kernel, then continue streaming full quality. that reduces perceived TTFT but can increase token cost and complicate client merging.
[04:38] Ethan: client merging is a concern - our app expects a single stream. we can handle stitched responses but it's extra work.
[04:44] Samir: understood. in the pilot we tried streaming stitch with a small 4-bit quant model for first token; it shaved ~120ms median TTFT in exchange for ~6% token overhead.
[04:57] Maya: that's promising. can you reproduce that on our VPC?
[05:01] Samir: yes, but we need representative traces, and to ensure quantized model math paths are available on your selected GPU. some vendor kernels don't support 4-bit fused-attn well.
[05:14] Maya: ah okay. how do we know which kernels exist on our instance types?
[05:18] Samir: we have a kernel matrix in the doc i sent last week; i'll re-share. it maps seqlen ranges and hardware to preferred kernels. but we should run a quick profiling pass on your machines to confirm.
[05:30] Avery: can you highlight the differences between fused-attn and matmul fallback in that matrix?
[05:35] Samir: sure. fused-attn is optimized for certain window sizes and reduces memory traffic; matmul fallback is more general but higher latency for small batches. fused-attn implementation often relies on specific cuda kernels that may be absent in older driver stacks.
[05:49] Li: we run fairly recent drivers but some of our hosts are on a conservative patch baseline. i can check driver versions and send exact gpu models.
[05:58] Ethan: we'll add that to the action list.
[06:02] Maya: do you have any quick wins for TTFT without changing infra?
[06:06] Samir: yes: small prompt trimming, prefer shorter initial prompts where possible, and enable prefix caching for shared context. also limit the batch hold window to 8ms instead of 20ms — that cut a bunch of TTFT in tests but increased GPU cycles marginally.
[06:20] Maya: prompt changes are product-impactful though. we can't always shorten prompts.
[06:24] Samir: understood. another option: hybrid route where we route first token to a tiny model hosted on CPU for instant reply while GPU warms; it's lower quality but sometimes acceptable.
[06:35] Maya: hmm, might be okay for certain UX flows. we'll need to review quality tradeoffs with product.
[06:42] Avery: let's park quality gating for now. next i want to talk about sequence length distribution you shared earlier; Samir did a quick bucketed heatmap?
[06:50] Samir: yes. your distribution: 60% under 128 tokens, 30% 128–512, 10% >512. but the p99 of length stretches beyond 1500 in long sessions. those rare long tails cause memory pressure and the runtime falls back to conservative kernels to avoid OOM.
[07:13] Li: the OOMs we saw were during synthetic load tests where we had several >1500 seqs concurrently. in production it's usually fewer but still spikes.
[07:23] Samir: for long tails we recommend aggressive quantization and offloading KV to a nearby host (sharded KV) to avoid per-instance memory spikes. that changes latency profile though.
[07:34] Ethan: does sharded KV add network hops?
[07:36] Samir: yes, adds a network hop per step when cache miss happens, so TTFT may increase slightly but steady-state token latency can be smoother across bursts.
[07:45] Maya: tradeoffs everywhere. can we simulate sharded KV in your cloud before doing it on our VPC?
[07:50] Samir: yeah we can run a demo in hosted and give you results, but it's better to run one on your exact topology for accurate numbers.
[07:58] Avery: quick check — any regulatory constraints about trace exports? maya?
[08:02] Maya: we can export anonymized traces, strip PII, shouldn't be a problem. security sign-off needed but ok.
[08:09] Samir: great. i'll need a 5k sample and we'll run the microburst profiling and a head-to-head kernel sweep.
[08:17] Ethan: timeline?
[08:19] Samir: i'll kick off profiling this week once we get the traces, expect 3–4 business days for detailed flamegraphs and per-kernel breakdowns.
[08:29] Maya: fine.
[08:30] (brief cross-talk)
[08:34] Li: one more infra note — autoscaler cooldowns can exacerbate microbursts because nodes spin up too slowly; we keep cooldown set to 120s; lowering helps with latency but may cause thrash.
[08:46] Samir: good point. part of the plan could be to tweak autoscaler thresholds for pilot to be more aggressive.
[08:53] Maya: are there recommendations for cooldown settings?
[08:55] Samir: usually 30–60s for low-latency services; depends on load pattern and cost tolerance. we can provide a suggested config.
[09:03] Avery: ok. let's walk through the kernel sweep approach quickly; Samir?
[09:07] Samir: the sweep will run three axes: seqlen bucket, batch size, and kernel variant (fused-attn, matmul fallback, quantized fused). for each cell we'll measure median TTFT, p95, and token-cost delta. we'll also capture memory pressure and any fallback events.
[09:23] Ethan: can it run without impacting production?
[09:25] Samir: yes — we run on shadowed traffic or a replay of anonymized traces on a staging cluster; we prefer staging that matches your node types.
[09:34] Maya: do you provide the run scripts?
[09:36] Samir: yes — we'll provide the harness and the perf spreadsheet.
[09:40] Avery: i'll send the harness links after the call.
[09:43] Maya: sounds good.
[09:45] Samir: quick callout: driver mismatch caused a weird 30% p95 regression on one of our customer's older nodes — so please confirm cuda/cuDNN versions.
[09:57] Li: will do.
[10:00] Avery: any blockers we should note?
[10:02] Maya: two: getting the 5k anonymized traces, and confirming a staging window where we can run the sweep.
[10:09] Ethan: we have a small staging pool we can open next Tuesday afternoon — i'll confirm.
[10:14] Samir: perfect. for customer expectations — after profiling we should have a recommendation: either tune batch window and autoscaler, or move to a reserved sticky pool, or enable hedged early-response. each has cost/quality tradeoffs; we'll quantify.
[10:30] Maya: timeline on that recommendation?
[10:32] Samir: 7 business days after we have traces and staging confirmation.
[10:37] Avery: ok. any other vendor comparisons to consider?
[10:40] Maya: product asked about MajorCloudAI's low-latency promise; they say auto-hedging built in. wondering if Redwood can show relative numbers.
[10:50] Samir: we'll include competitor frame-of-reference where public numbers exist, but direct apples-to-apples requires same traces. we can run a short three-way on hosted for a high-level view.
[11:00] Ethan: that would help.
[11:03] Avery: recap — Samir will run microburst profiling and kernel sweep once Maya drops traces; Ethan confirm staging window; Li provide driver/GPU list; Avery share docs and pricing. we'll schedule kernel decision meeting week of 2027-01-17.
[11:20] Maya: thanks all. one last Q — is there an easy way to detect when a request hit matmul fallback in logs?
[11:28] Samir: yes, our runtime emits a kernel id tag in the trace (sometimes labelled kern_id in older stacks). it shows fallback and cache-miss events; i'll include the log parsing snippet.
[11:40] Li: that'll be helpful for triage.
[11:44] Avery: great. finishing notes — i will send the deck and perf matrix, samir will share profiling template. any final comments?
[11:54] Maya: nope, thanks everyone.
[11:56] Ethan: thanks.
[11:58] (call ends)

Recap (end):
- Deliverables: microburst profiling with flamegraphs (Samir), anonymized traces (Maya), staging window confirmation (Ethan), driver/GPU list (Li), docs/pricing (Avery).
- Next meeting: kernel decision workshop week of 2027-01-17 (Avery to propose times).

References shared during call:
- Kernel perf matrix: https://redwood.company/docs/kernel-matrix
